subject: AI & Agents
title: The Second AI Winter
description: A fast breakdown of The Second AI Winter for builders.

hook.text: In the late 1980s, companies poured billions into AI expert systems. Most went bankrupt.

buildup.text: Specialized AI hardware companies like Lisp Machines Inc. collapsed as PCs got cheaper.

discovery.text: Expert systems couldn't scale. Maintaining thousands of hand-coded rules was a nightmare.

twist.text: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Project, a $400 million bet on AI, failed to meet its goals.

climax.text: By 1993, 'AI' became a dirty word. Researchers rebranded their work as 'machine learning.'

punchline.text: Same science, new name, less baggage.

quiz.question: Why did the second AI winter happen?
options: Expert systems couldn't scale and AI hardware companies collapsed

details.summary: The second AI winter in the late 1980s and 1990s followed the collapse of the expert systems market. Companies discovered that maintaining rule-based AI was too expensive and brittle for commercial use.
details.whyItMatters: The second winter reinforced lessons about sustainable AI commercialization. The pattern of overpromising commercial value and underdelivering continues to be relevant in today's AI boom.
takeaways: Expert systems failed commercially in the late 1980s
Maintenance costs and brittleness made them impractical
The cycle of hype and disappointment repeated with similar causes

faq.question: What caused the second AI winter?
faq.answer: Companies invested heavily in expert systems expecting transformative business value. But these systems were expensive to maintain, could not handle edge cases, and delivered less value than promised.

faq.question: How did AI recover from the second winter?
faq.answer: Statistical methods and machine learning gradually replaced rule-based approaches. Increased data availability and computing power in the 2000s enabled new successes that rebuilt confidence in AI research.
